zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-check for this three-page review: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510 (CC BY 4.0), supplied with the input package. Dataset: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Consulted after independent readings; the native BnF scans govern the diplomatic text.

runs.text: Tomar poße da rẽda, ou terras a primeira vez.

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry: taking possession of a revenue or estate for the first time. The initial verb is Tomar, and the damaged contracted noun is read as rẽda, not OCR rẽla; the printed abbreviation is not expanded.

runs.text: O entrar, ou misturarſe hũa couſa cõ

lines.note: Nyuuka denotes one thing entering or becoming mixed with another. The entry's territorial example below supports this sense, rather than the OCR's malformed initial Xh; the Portuguese verb is misturarſe.

runs.text: outra: particularmente ſe diz de terras de hum

lines.note: Outra completes the reciprocal relation of two things. The gloss then narrows the application to one lord's lands, continuing into the next row.

runs.text: ſenhor que entrão pollas do outro. Vt,

lines.note: The lands of one lord extend into those of another. Vt introduces nyuuka suru, divided after Nhǔ- at the visible line-end mark.
Completes nyuuka suru, the verbal expression illustrating the preceding entry. This short Japanese continuation is a separate physical row, with no additional Portuguese translation.
Nyuukoo is glossed simply as incense. Both the u and o carry downward-pointing marks in this impression; the spelling is preserved independently of modern vowel notation.
Nyuukoku is explained by kuni ni iru, entering a country or domain. The Portuguese specifies the first entry, whose circumstances continue below.

runs.text: no reino depois de tomado, ou conquiſtado,

lines.note: The first entry follows taking or conquering the realm. This is a continuation of nyuukoku, not a separate military headword; the scan supports the contiguous depois.

runs.text: ou dado po lo ſenhor da Tenca, &c.

lines.note: Alternatively the domain has been granted by the ruler of the realm. Tenca is Japanese embedded in the italic Portuguese explanation. At po lo a weak intervening trace could be a damaged additional l; the aligned draft's spacing and single l are retained instead of confidently supplying pollo.
Nyuudoo, explained as doo ni iru, is glossed as a shaven person, that is, one who has taken the tonsure. The headword's second letter is h, not OCR n; the example begins at the right edge.
Completes nyuudoo suru, taking the tonsure or becoming shaven. The Portuguese reflexive phrase belongs to this example, not to the next entry with the same headword spelling.
This separate nyuudoo entry means entering a temple hall, explained by doo ye iru. The Portuguese has the Japanese temple word Tera within its sentence; fa- continues as fazer below.
Completes fazer oração: the temple is entered in order to pray. The two-word continuation belongs to the second nyuudoo entry.
Nyuudoogumo names a kind of large spider. The scan supplies a mark over u missing from the draft; no modern species identification is imposed on the description.

runs.text: des, que tem o corpo redondo.

lines.note: Completes grandes and specifies that these spiders have a round body. This physical description closes the preceding entry.
Nyuujoo is explained by joo ni iru. The dictionary's gloss concerns voluntarily entering fire or another place to die; the initial N and the verb iru correct OCR X and uru.

runs.text: baixo da terra, ou nagoa tomando a morte por

lines.note: Continues with going beneath the earth or into water and voluntarily accepting death. De above joins baixo here syntactically; the printed nagoa is retained without expansion.

runs.text: ſi como fazem algũs Bonzos gentios.

lines.note: Completes por si and attributes the practice to certain non-Christian Buddhist monks. This is the dictionary's historical explanation, including its religious vocabulary, rather than a modern definition of all uses of nyuujoo.
Nyuumet, with a checked final t, is defined as the death of a Buddha. Fotoque is Japanese embedded within the Portuguese gloss; it is not a second headword.

runs.text: Nhǔmi. Chino agiuai. i, Amaqi agiuai.

lines.note: Nyuumi is paraphrased as chi no ajiwai and amaki ajiwai, the taste of milk and a sweet taste. The Portuguese gloss on the next row identifies milk; the mark over the headword's u is read as a caron.
Leite gives the milk sense explicitly. Nyuumi wo nomu means drinking milk, exactly matching beber leite.
Nyuunan is identified with yawaraka, softness or gentleness. The Portuguese gives both mildness and meekness, rather than the modern technical sense of flexibility alone.
Nyuunanna is the adjectival form associated with gentleness. Its weakened u and mark are supported by the repeated form in the example; the draft's Nhinanna would misidentify the word.
Completes nyuunanna hito, a meek and gentle person. The divided headword is not an independent nanna entry.
Nyuutsu is explained by minato ye iru, entering a port. Vt introduces the formal verbal example on the next row.

Nyuutsu tsukamatsuru is a deferential way of saying that one enters a port. The weak mark over u is retained as the draft's grave; damage prevents securely excluding a caron, so it is not harmonized with the preceding headword.
Nyuuwa denotes gentleness. The Japanese paraphrase repeats yawaraka; the first capital is Y, not OCR T, and the headword begins N rather than R.
Nyuuwa ninniku no hito describes a gentle, patient person. Ninniku here is forbearance, as the Portuguese continuation makes clear, not the unrelated garlic word.
Completes mã-ſo and supplies paciente, closing the explanation of the gentle and forbearing person.
Nyuuwa na is adjectival, describing someone meek or mild in temperament. The damaged initial is N; the Portuguese concerns disposition rather than material softness.
Nyuuwa ninniku combines gentleness with patient forbearance. The visible space between the two Japanese elements is retained; the final Portuguese com governs paciencia below.
Paciencia completes the compound's explanation as gentleness with patience. This final row precedes the new alphabetical subsection, rather than belonging to its heading.

Ni is identified as a dative particle. The opening N is an enlarged initial spanning two physical rows, followed by capital I; the OCR pilcrow is not printed text. Datiuo, not Daiuo, names the grammatical case.

A second use of ni is described as an ablative preposition. Preserve the printed Propoſição rather than replacing it with an expected modern grammatical term; the line is indented beside the enlarged N above.
The noun ni means a load or baggage. Ni wo tsumu illustrates loading it; Portuguese Ar- begins arrumar across the physical line break.
Completes arranging the baggage aboard a vessel. Ni wo no- begins the next loading expression, nosuru, which continues below.
Nosuru means putting baggage aboard. Ni wo orosu then introduces unloading; initial v in voroſu belongs to the historical romanization and is not a separate syllable.

runs.text: Deſembarcar o fato, ou deſcarregar a besta.

lines.note: Translates ni wo orosu as taking baggage off a vessel or unloading a pack animal. Both alternatives belong to the same example.
Ni wo oosuru is illustrated by loading a beast or an ox. The circumflex belongs to the Japanese verb, and the historical spelling boy remains unchanged.

Ni wo oo and the alternative kataguru mean carrying baggage on one's shoulders. Latin l marks the alternative; the final Portuguese word is às, continuing with costas below, not the draft's à plus a full stop.
Costas completes the preceding carrying expression. Nijirushi is then a mark identifying baggage; q̃ is the printed contraction introducing the following relative clause.
The identifying mark is placed on the baggage. Ni ni motanu introduces the figurative expression explained below as taking no notice or concern.

runs.text: fazer caſo, ou não ſe lhe dar nada.

lines.note: Completes the negative translation of ni ni motanu: not to care or make anything of it. This idiomatic gloss is distinct from physically failing to carry a load.
Ni, niru, nita is the verb for cooking or boiling over a fire. The abbreviated principal parts are preserved rather than expanded in the transcription.

This homographic verb means resembling or being similar, not cooking. The scan supports Ni and the full past ending ita, and recovers the Portuguese resemblance gloss from the severely garbled OCR; its example continues at the top of column 2.
Oya ni nita ko illustrates the resemblance verb at the foot of column 1: a child resembling a parent. Initial V in Voyani is retained as printed, not read as an additional syllable.
The parent may be the child's father or mother. This continuation completes the resemblance example rather than starting the following plant entry.

runs.text: Erua como anil de tingir dazul.

lines.note: Niai names an herb compared with indigo and used for dyeing blue. The gloss provides the dyeing function but does not by itself establish a precise modern botanical identification.
Niai and its principal forms mean fitting, suiting, or being appropriate. This verbal entry is distinct from the identically spelled plant name above.

runs.text: Couſa que quadra, ou he conueniente.

lines.note: Niai no describes something that fits or is suitable. The Portuguese restates the adjectival use of the preceding verb.
Nibe is a fish compared with corvina. The historical Portuguese u/v spelling is retained, without claiming that the comparison determines a modern species.

runs.text: Certo grude forte com que pegão as ca-

lines.note: A separate nibe entry denotes a strong adhesive. Its use in fastening the bow's cane components continues onto the next row.
Completes canas do arco, the cane or bamboo parts of the bow. The short continuation explains the adhesive's application.

runs.text: Homem que tem cuidado do fato.

lines.note: Nibugyoo is the person responsible for baggage. The gloss expresses an assigned responsibility, not merely someone carrying an individual load.
Nibui describes slowness or sluggishness. The first example starts with the divided adjective Ni-bui and applies it to a horse.
Nibui uma is a slow horse. The following repetition of Nibui begins the example concerning a person on the next row.
Nibui hito is a slow person, also explained as someone intellectually dull. The second Portuguese characterization continues below.
Tardo de engenho specifies slowness of understanding. It completes the human example and is not a further Japanese form.
Nibuu and nibusa supply the adverbial and nominal forms associated with nibui. They are printed without a fresh Portuguese definition.
Nikai is an upper storey. Nikaizukuri no iye illustrates a house built with an upper floor; the doubled z sequence is retained.
Translates the preceding house example as a house constructed with an upper storey. This is the building sense of sobrado.

runs.text: Colla que ſe faz de pelle de vaca co-

lines.note: Nikawa is glue made from cowhide. The adjective describing the hide is divided co-zida across the line break.
Completes cozida: the cowhide is boiled to make the glue. This one-word continuation remains a physical body line.
Nicchuu means at midday. The Portuguese retains the historical meo spelling, and the Japanese u bears a downward mark.
Nikko and nikkoto denote a manner of smiling. The scan shows two c types in Nicco, unlike OCR Nico; Latin l introduces the alternative adverbial form.
Nikkorito is another smiling expression. Idem refers back to the adverbial description in the preceding entry.
Nichigwat is paraphrased by hi and tsuki, sun and moon. The final t is the historical checked ending, not an omitted modern syllable to restore.
Nichigen, explained as hi no kagiri, concerns fixing a day or time limit. The Portuguese construction continues with certo below.
Nichigen wo sadamuru, alternatively sasu, means setting a definite day. The second verb is visibly divided at the right edge.

runs.text: Determinar, ou apontar algũ dia certo.

lines.note: Completes sasu and translates both alternatives as determining or appointing a particular day. The contracted algũ is not expanded.
Nichi nichi is equated with hibi ni, every day. The scan's separate Nichi nichi is preserved rather than joined as a normalized compound.
Nichirin denotes the sun, literally the solar disc in the Japanese compound. The printed gloss itself is only Sol.
Nichiya means day and night. Nichiya no begins a quotation about continuous vigilance on the following row.
Yoojin hima nakarikereba describes there being no respite from vigilance by day and night. Taif. is the upright citation label; Lib. begins the italic book reference continued below.

runs.text: 29. Não fazião ſe não vigiar de di, a &

lines.note: Book 29 is followed by a translation saying that they did nothing but keep watch. The intrusive comma in printed di, a is retained as an apparent typographical anomaly within the intended word dia, not silently moved to modern punctuation.
De noite completes the day-and-night vigilance translation. This short continuation closes the quotation.
Nichiyoo is here defined as the influence of the sun. The circumflex distinguishes the printed mark from the carons in nearby entries; this is not the preceding nichiya word.

Nichuu is paraphrased by mimi no uchi, inside the ears. The Japanese explanation and Portuguese gloss agree on location within the ear, despite possible modern expectations about the compound's reading.
Nikoo is a shaven woman, in the religious context a tonsured woman. The gloss uses the historical Molher spelling and does not supply a separate institutional title.

runs.text: Certos limos, ou folhas largas do mar

lines.note: Nikobu denotes a preparation of broad seaweed fronds. The final word cozidas on the next row establishes that they are cooked, rather than naming a raw plant alone.
Cozidas completes the seaweed definition: the broad marine leaves are boiled or cooked. It is a genuine one-word body continuation.

runs.text: Callo, ou polmão q̃ ſe faz ao derredor

lines.note: This separate nikobu is a callus or swelling. The historical Portuguese polmão is retained as printed; the anatomical location and cause follow below.

runs.text: do peſcoço aos que carretão fato.

lines.note: The swelling forms around the neck of people who carry baggage. This identifies a load-bearing callus, not the cooked-seaweed homograph above.

Nikon is explained by mimi no ne and denotes the faculty of hearing or the ears themselves. The final syllable of ouuidos is divided across the next row; the Japanese compound is not emended from its damaged n shapes.
Completes ouuidos, ears. The closing S. is a separate upright written-register label, not part of the italic Portuguese noun.
Nikonikoto is an adverb describing smiling. The Portuguese gives the manner and introduces a verbal example below; the close-set deſe is retained.
Nikonikoto waroo means smiling or laughing with a cheerful expression. The final Japanese vowel has a caron in the scan.
Nikonikoto shite is another construction with the same smiling sense. The example begins here and supplies the following verb on the next row.
Nikonikoto shite iru describes being or remaining smiling. Portuguese estar-se sorrindo translates that continuing state; the historical ſurrindo spelling is preserved.
Nikoyakana describes something cheerful. The example repeats the adjective across a visible line-end division before hito below.
Completes nikoyakana hito, a cheerful or smiling person. The explanatory Portuguese riſonho is retained with its visible long s.
Nikoyakani is the corresponding adverbial form. Adu. supplies only its grammatical classification, relying on the preceding cheerful-person entry for meaning.
